To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross-sectional analyses do not distinguish benign from carcinatous human prostate, but paired analyses of carcinomatous and benign tissue of the same gland do.

(1) cross-sectional analyses of cytoplasm and nucleus androgen receptor content cannot distinguish benign from carcinatous human prostate; (2) the cytoplasm and nuclear androgen receptors of carcinatous prostate may be increased or unchanged compared to noncarcinomatou prostate from the same gland; (3) these results may reflect a difference between the androgen receptor of carcinatous and noncarcinosatous prostatic cells.
cross-sectional analyses failed to distinguish benign from malignant human prostate but that paired analyses did.

the role of the androgen receptor in the pathogenesis and treatment of prostatic carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the androgen receptor content and its cytoplasmic versus nuclear localization are not reliable indicators of prostatic malignancy in the human prostate.
the inability of cytoplasm or nucleus to distinguish benign from malignant prostate does not necessarily preclude their ability to distinguish malignant from benign prostate.
cross-sectional analyses do not distinguish between benign and malignant prostatic tissue; whereas, paired analyses do.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
androgen receptor content is not a reliable predictor of prostatic carcinoma.
cytoplasmic receptor content, nuclear receptor content, and cytoplasmic to nuclear receptor content ratios fail to distinguish carcinomata from noncarcinomata of human prostate.

, in the absence of other information, cross-sectional analyses of receptor content fail to discriminate benign from malignant prostate; but that paired analyses of these two tissues in the same gland may be of value in distinguishing benign from malignant prostate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
androgen receptor content is not a reliable indicator of the status of prostate cancer, either in terms of the presence of disease or its aggressiveness.
androgen receptor content is a poor predictor of prostate cancer.
the androgen receptor status of a prostate biopsy specimen cannot be used to distinguish benign from malignant disease.
